source_text: Huius igitur paenitentiae secundae et unius quanto in arto negotium est, tanto operosior probatio, ut non sola conscientia praeferatur, sed aliquo etiam actu administretur. Is actus, qui magis Graeco vocabulo exprimitur et frequentatur, exomologesis est, qua delictum domino nostrum confitemur, non quidem ut ignaro, sed quatenus satisfactio confessione disponitur, confessione paenitentia nascitur, paenitentia deus mitigatur. Itaque exomologesis prosternendi et humilificandi hominis disciplina est, conversationem iniungens misericordiae illicem. De ipso quoque habite atque victu mandat sacco et cineri incubare, corpus sordibus obscurare, animum maeroribus deiicere, illa quae peccavit tristi tractatione mutare, ceterum pastum et potum pura nosse, non ventris scilicet, sed animae causa, plerumque vero ieiuniis preces alere, ingemiscere, lacrimari et mugire dies noctesque ad dominum deum tuum, presbyteris advolvi, et caris dei adgeniculari, omnibus fratribus legationes deprecationis suae iniungere. Haec omnia exomologesis, ut paenitentiam commendet, ut de periculi timore dominum honoret, ut in peccatorem ipsa pronuntians pro dei indignatione fungatur et temporali afflictatione aeterna supplicia, non dicam frustretur, sed expungat. Cum igitur provolvit hominem, magis relevat; cum squalidum facit, magis mundatum reddit; cum accusat, excusat; cum condemnat, absolvit. In quantum non peperceris tibi, in tantum tibi deus, crede, parcet.
orientation: Tertullian is explaining how the one second repentance after baptism must be carried out, namely through the public discipline of exomologesis.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, of this second repentance and single one, how much the business is in a narrow place, so much more laborious is the proving, so that not only conscience may be brought forward, but it may also be administered by some act. This act, which is expressed and practiced more by the Greek word, is public confession, by which we confess our sin to the Lord, not indeed as to one ignorant, but insofar as making amends is arranged by confession, by confession repentance is born, by repentance God is appeased. And so public confession is a discipline of prostrating and humbling a person, enjoining a manner of life that entices mercy. Also concerning dress itself and food it commands to lie in sackcloth and ashes, to darken the body with filth, to cast down the spirit with sorrows, to change by sad treatment those things which it sinned, moreover to know food and drink as pure, not for the belly's sake, of course, but for the soul's sake, but very often to nourish prayers with fasts, to groan, to weep and to bellow days and nights to the Lord your God, to fall down before the presbyters, and to kneel before the dear ones of God, to enjoin on all the brothers the embassies of one's own entreaty. All these things public confession does, in order that it may commend repentance, in order that it may honor the Lord from fear of danger, in order that, itself pronouncing against the sinner, it may act in place of God's indignation and by temporal affliction may not, I shall not say cheat, but blot out eternal punishments. When therefore it throws a person down, it lifts him up more; when it makes him filthy, it gives him back more cleansed; when it accuses, it excuses; when it condemns, it acquits. Insofar as you will not have spared yourself, so far God, believe, will spare you.

pass_b_english: This second repentance is a single one, and the narrower its ground, the more demanding its proof. It must not be carried only in the conscience, but also performed in some outward act. That act, which is better expressed and more often practiced by a Greek word, is public confession. Through it we confess our sin to the Lord—not as if He did not know it, but because making amends is set in motion by confession, repentance is born from confession, and God is appeased by repentance.

Public confession, therefore, is a discipline of prostrating and humbling a person, imposing a manner of life that entices mercy. It commands the sinner to lie in sackcloth and ashes, to darken the body with filth, to cast down the spirit with grief, to exchange for harsh treatment whatever one has sinned with. For food and drink it prescribes what is pure—not for the belly's sake, of course, but for the soul's. Most often it nourishes prayer with fasts, groaning, weeping, and bellowing day and night to the Lord your God, falling before the presbyters, kneeling before God's beloved, and charging all the brothers and sisters to carry the embassies of one's own entreaty.

Public confession does all this to make repentance commendable, to honor the Lord through fear of danger, to stand in for God's indignation by pronouncing sentence against the sinner, and by temporal affliction not—I will not say to frustrate—but to wipe out eternal punishments. When it throws a person down, it lifts him up more; when it makes him filthy, it returns him more cleansed; when it accuses, it excuses; when it condemns, it absolves. To the degree you have not spared yourself, believe that God will spare you.

problems.quote: not—I will not say to cheat—but to cancel eternal punishments
problems.why: frustretur means "to be frustrated", not "to cheat".
problems.fix: not—I will not say "frustrated"—but to wipe out eternal punishments
problems.ruling: frustretur means 'to frustrate/thwart'; 'to cheat' misleads the reader about evading punishment.

edits.old: not—I will not say to cheat—but to cancel eternal punishments
edits.new: not—I will not say to frustrate—but to wipe out eternal punishments

fixed: Changed 'to cheat' to 'to frustrate' and 'to cancel' to 'to wipe out' to match the source 'frustretur' and 'expungat'.

problems.why: Latin specifies ‘pure’ food and drink, not merely ‘plain’.
problems.ruling: pura means 'pure', not 'plain'; the distinction between pure and plain food matters for the penitential discipline.

edits.old: For food and drink it prescribes what is plain—not for the belly's sake, of course, but for the soul's.
edits.new: For food and drink it prescribes what is pure—not for the belly's sake, of course, but for the soul's.

fixed: Changed 'what is plain' to 'what is pure' because the source 'pura nosse' specifies pure food and drink, not merely plain.

last_rejected.quote: imposing a manner of life that entices mercy
last_rejected.why: Latin says the conduct is illicit (illicem), not that it entices mercy.
last_rejected.fix: imposing an illicit way of life of mercy
last_rejected.ruling: illicem is from illicere 'to entice/attract'; misericordiae illicem = 'lure/enticement of mercy', not 'illicit'.

last_rejected.why: advolvi means to rush to or hurry to, not to fall before.
last_rejected.ruling: advolvi can mean 'to throw oneself at/before'; 'falling before' fits context of prostration before presbyters.

polish.changed: Clarified the Greek term as public confession, identified presbyters as church elders, and smoothed sentence flow while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: which is better expressed and more often practiced by a Greek word
notes.why: The Greek word (exomologesis) is alluded to but never given; reader cannot identify it.
notes.fix: Supply the word: 'the Greek word exomologesis.'

notes.why: Modern reader may not know this is the office of church elders/priests.
